key_insight: In a simplified recorder mouthpiece, mouth distance most strongly controls jet oscillations: Stage I frequency scales inversely with distance, and longer distances introduce a second oscillation stage.
engineering_relevance: Mouthpiece geometry offers a way to tune jet frequency and oscillation strength before accounting for coupling to an instrument’s acoustic resonator.
method: Run over 200 two-dimensional direct numerical simulations using an immersed boundary method.
Vary mouth distance, labium angle, vertical offset, and Reynolds number.
Characterize oscillation regimes through transverse-force spectra on the labium.
evidence_signal: The baseline exhibits Stage I oscillations at St ≈ 0.07, nearly constant for Re ≥ 330; a second stage becomes established at 6.5 windway heights and dominant from 8.
watch_item: The two-dimensional, resonator-free model isolates hydrodynamics but does not establish behavior in a full three-dimensional instrument with acoustic feedback.
paper_title: Hydrodynamic regimes of the edge-tone in a simplified recorder mouthpiece
